output.title: The Cutting of the String
output.prologue: The sky once lay close over the islands, held by a single string that Mother Hesk wound at the pole. Aun wanted to know how far the wind went, so he cut it. This is the telling of that cut, as the year turns. Start at the Spindle, where Hesk still keeps count. Go out along the Lamp Road, where the Sun-Kite flies and its ribbon trails. End in the Unflown, where things lost go and nobody comes back to say what they found. Tell it low, with your hands busy.

stops.text: Mother Hesk sat at the pole with her spindle, drawing the string out thin so the islands would not drift. She wound it on the whorl and counted each turn. Aun came up the cliff with his knife in his teeth and a kite under one arm. He asked her how far the wind went. Hesk did not look up. She had heard the question before, from gulls and from goats, and she kept winding.

Hesk keeps count, and she did not like what she was counting. The string was thinner in her hands, and the knots she had tied for every child of the islands were slipping toward the cut. So at the new moon she called the kite-makers up to the cliff. Fly the Tally Kite, she said. Let the wind count the knots for me. The wind counted, and the number was short.

When Aun cut the string, the sky ran up so fast the year's sailcloth nearly tore off the Reel. Hesk was quick. She put her weight on the loom-stone and held the cloth down, the way a woman holds a net on a windy shingle. Her knuckles went white. Aun saw her hold it and laughed, and that was the first time he was sorry, though it was not the last.

When Aun cut the string and the sky went up, he was thirsty, as all Fliers are, having shouted at the wind since noon. He had no bottle. He had only the bag of goat-skin he used for his kite-cloth, and he drank from the wrong end of it. Salt water came up the neck and he spat it at the wind, which spat it back. Thirst is a poor reason for a cut, but it is the one the old women give.

The rope that held the sky came apart in Aun's hands, and the sky went up with its ends frayed, like a sail after a bad season. Hesk sent the Gulls down to say so. They came over the cliffs in a grey chorus, shrieking the news into every chimney. Aun had expected anger. What he got was the Gulls' flat, patient voices, and a fid, the bone pricker, pushed into his palm. Mend what you can, they said.

Aun tied the first knot in the Lamp Road's cord the day he wondered how many days a pair of hands could work before they gave out. He tied one knot for every day his hands had worked. The belt grew heavy at his hip, and when it caught on the sail-ropes he swore, then counted, then fell quiet. The count ran longer than he hoped. He had already learned that a sky could not be wound back, but a belt could be worn.

When Aun cut the string he did not cut it clean. The last of it hung from the Sun-Kite's tail, and Ennu the Kite-Wright sewed the Sun-Kite from old sailcloth so the end could ride the Lamp Road all year without tearing free. His fingers went numb in the cold, so he stitched with his teeth. He told Aun a kite is only as true as its last knot. Aun did not ask what he meant. It was not the last thing he failed to ask.

Ennu sewed the bride's kite the night before his daughter's wedding, with sailcloth, goat-gut, and a gull's wing-bone for the spar. He worked by the hearth until the fire was grey. When the kite was done he could not look at it. He flew it once, at dawn, so the girl would have something to take across the water. Then he went back to the cloth. The wind was still wind, and he had a second kite to make.

The Sun-Kite was still tied to Aun's wrist when the knife came down, so it went up with the others. Its ribbon came loose and streamed out behind it, a long red thread across the dark, and the Gulls said it was the only lamp that flew with a tail to show which way it turned. Aun held his wrist up to the sky. The ribbon was all that was left of his hand on the Lamp Road.

Aun cut the string because he wanted to know how far the wind went. The sky drifted off with him still holding the knife, and every kite he had flown on that string went with it, pulling against nothing. He had meant to fly one more. He stood on the ledge with the cut end in his fist, and the wind, which had always answered him, said nothing at all. The old men still fly it when they want a reason to be angry at him.

When a child goes into the sea, the mother climbs to the cliff on the first still day, when the wind has let go of the water. She ties a small kite of sailcloth to a long line and lets it out, knot after knot, until it is a speck over the Unflown. Then she reels it in. The child is not on the line. Still, she keeps the line, and the old women say the kite goes on past the last lamp to look.

Ithúna went down to the Skarel rocks one grey morning after the goats, and the sea took her before anyone saw. Her mother could not bury what she had not been given back. So she parted the string at the reel and let the kite go, so there would be a line somewhere that ran to the drowned. The string never came back. It is still out there, unwound, and Hesk has not counted it.

Ennu sat on the cliff with a bone needle and a bolt of sailcloth, making a gull for a woman whose husband had gone out in a boat and not come back. He sewed the wings on loose, so the gull could leave when it liked. He left the last seam open too. A gull should be able to go and come back, he said. She took it up the cliff and let it go into the Unflown, where things lost go to be unstitched.

When Aun cut the string, the sky went up, and the dead went with it as kites. But the Unflown lies past where the wind comes back, and there the dead do not stay put. They fly with no line to hold them. Nasmi is the rope that was never laid, the one Hesk had meant to twist for the boats. Sailors who go far enough south say they hear it humming, the way a rope hums when it is pulled taut by nothing at all.

When Aun cut the string, the sky went up but did not come all the way free. A short length of cord stayed knotted to his hand, and it still hangs from the bottom of the sky, where the Unflown begins. Aun has never been able to let go of it. Whoever holds the end feels the sky pull, faint and cold, like a fish that has not decided. Hesk does not ask for it back. A cut, she says, is only half a sentence.
